planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost in warm soil and transplant out after all frost danger has passed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; habanero needs consistent heat and a long growing season to fully ripen and develop maximum heat and fruitiness.

directions: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost in warm soil and transplant out after all frost danger has passed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; habanero needs consistent heat and a long growing season to fully ripen and develop maximum heat and fruitiness. This classic habanero selection produces small, lantern-shaped fruit that ripens from green through yellow to a vivid bright orange, carrying an intense, fruity, floral heat in the 100,000-350,000 Scoville range that has made habanero peppers a staple of Caribbean, Yucatecan, and hot sauce cuisine. The compact, bushy plants are heavy producers over a long season and thrive in the same hot, humid conditions favored by many tropical Capsicum species, continuing to set fruit through the hottest part of summer when some other peppers slow down. Harvest fruit at full orange color for maximum heat and flavor, wear gloves when handling, and avoid touching your face or eyes after working with the fruit.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Irish lace marigold forms a low, dense mound of finely divided, thread-like foliage and needs no staking.

directions: Direct sow after last frost into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Irish lace marigold forms a low, dense mound of finely divided, thread-like foliage and needs no staking. Extremely fine, feathery, fern-like foliage carries a strong anise or licorice fragrance and flavor when crushed, used in parts of Mexico and Central America as a culinary herb and traditional flavoring, quite different from the coarser leaves and stronger, more medicinal scent of common marigold species. Tiny, inconspicuous white flowers appear over a long season, but this species is grown chiefly for its ornamental, lacy foliage texture and edible, licorice-scented leaves rather than a showy floral display. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once established, it makes a fine edging plant or herb-garden filler, and harvested leaves can be used fresh or dried as a licorice-flavored seasoning.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products
Slow Food International Ark of Taste

planting.note: Plant transplants after last frost in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; guinea hen weed is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 9-11.

directions: Plant transplants after last frost in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; guinea hen weed is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 9-11. Slender, upright stems carry narrow leaves with a distinctive strong garlic-like smell when crushed or bruised, topped with thin spikes of small white flowers, and the whole plant, known as anamu across the Caribbean and tropical Latin America, is widely used in traditional folk medicine for a range of purported benefits, though rigorous clinical evidence remains limited. Easy to grow in warm, humid climates, it spreads readily by both seed and root suckers once established, sometimes naturalizing in disturbed ground in frost-free regions. Harvest leaves and roots for traditional preparations as needed, but consult a healthcare provider before using medicinally, since it has documented interactions and safety concerns, particularly during pregnancy.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products
Slow Food International Ark of Taste

planting.note: Plant transplants after last frost in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; day jessamine self-sows readily in warm climates and its white berries are toxic if ingested, so site away from grazing animals and small children.

directions: Plant transplants after last frost in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; day jessamine self-sows readily in warm climates and its white berries are toxic if ingested, so site away from grazing animals and small children. Clusters of small, tubular, greenish-white flowers open by day, unlike the related night-blooming jessamine, releasing a mild, sweet fragrance through the daylight hours before giving way to small white berries that persist into fall and winter. Native to the Caribbean and long naturalized across the Gulf South, it grows quickly into a loose, twiggy shrub tolerant of a range of soils and light conditions, but its toxic berries have caused documented livestock poisoning in Florida cattle, so it is not recommended near pastures. Prune to control size and self-sowing, and remove volunteer seedlings promptly in naturalistic areas to prevent it from spreading beyond the intended planting.

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; trumpet tree is a frost-tender, fast-growing pioneer species realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse.

directions: Plant seedlings in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; trumpet tree is a frost-tender, fast-growing pioneer species realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. Large, distinctive, deeply lobed, umbrella-like leaves radiate from hollow, jointed stems on this extremely fast-growing Neotropical pioneer tree, which colonizes disturbed clearings and forest gaps throughout Central and South America, its hollow stems famously providing a home for symbiotic Azteca ants that protect the tree from herbivores in exchange for shelter and food. Growing many feet per year when young, it is one of the fastest-growing woody trees in the American tropics but is relatively short-lived and structurally weak, better suited to quickly establishing shade or a distinctive architectural specimen in a tropical garden than a long-term landscape anchor. Water regularly while young, provide full sun for the fastest growth, and expect a relatively short lifespan compared to slower, longer-lived tropical trees.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; guaba is a frost-tender rainforest and riverbank tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; guaba is a frost-tender rainforest and riverbank tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. Closely related to and grown much like the more familiar ice cream bean, this fast-growing tropical legume tree produces long, ribbed pods containing seeds wrapped in the same soft, sweet, cotton-candy-like white pulp eaten fresh straight from the pod across Central and South America, though its pods and pulp are typically somewhat smaller than its larger relative. As a nitrogen-fixing legume it enriches surrounding soil and is commonly used as a fast-growing shade tree in coffee and cacao agroforestry systems throughout its native range. Water regularly, especially while young, and expect a few years of growth before the tree reaches significant pod production.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; physic nut is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. All parts of the plant, especially the seeds, are toxic if ingested, so site away from children and pets.

directions: Plant seedlings in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; physic nut is frost-tender and realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. All parts of the plant, especially the seeds, are toxic if ingested, so site away from children and pets. Thick, succulent stems and broad, lobed leaves cover a fast-growing, drought-tolerant shrub long used as a living fence across the tropics for its ease of propagation from simple stem cuttings, more recently studied worldwide as a source of biodiesel from the high oil content of its toxic seeds. Extremely tough and drought-tolerant once established, it thrives on poor, marginal soils with minimal care, but every part of the plant, particularly the oil-rich seeds, contains toxic compounds that cause severe illness if ingested by people or animals. Grow it as a hedge or specimen shrub in a location away from curious children, pets, or livestock, and handle pruned material with gloves, since the sap can irritate skin.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products
